title: Architecture analysis: Build-time dependency installation via build_commands in repositories.yaml
summary: Add a `build_commands` configuration section to per-repo settings in `repositories.yaml` that allows users to specify dependency installation commands (e.g. `npm ci`, `pip install -r requirements.txt`) to run during the Docker image build phase. Watch files (e.g. lockfiles) are copied into the build context to enable Docker layer caching — deps only rebuild when watch files change. All repos' dependencies coexist in the single `egg` image. The recommended approach extends the existing `docker-setup.py` build script to handle `build_commands` for each repo, adds a new Dockerfile layer that copies watch files before running the build script, and extends `compute_build_hash()` to include watch file contents.

problem_statement.description: In private mode, the sandbox container has no network access beyond the Anthropic API. Dependencies cannot be installed at runtime — pip install, npm install, etc. all fail. The existing `docker_setup.extra_packages` config only supports OS-level apt/dnf packages during image build. There is no mechanism for project-specific dependency installation (Python venvs, node_modules, Go modules) that requires repo-specific files like lockfiles or Makefiles.
constraints: All dependencies must be baked into the single `egg` Docker image — no per-repo images
Docker layer caching must be leveraged so dependency layers are only rebuilt when watch files change
Only watch files (not full repos) are copied during build — full repos are mounted at runtime
Backwards compatible — repos without `build_commands` are unaffected
Commands run as root during build, same as existing `docker-setup.py` execution context
Must work with the existing build hash system to detect when rebuilds are needed

current_architecture.build_pipeline_overview: The Docker build pipeline is orchestrated by `sandbox/egg_lib/docker.py`. The `build_image()` function checks `should_rebuild_image()` (using content hashing), then calls `create_dockerfile()` to stage files into `~/.cache/egg/`, and finally runs `docker build`. The `compute_build_hash()` function hashes all build-affecting files to determine if a rebuild is needed. The hash is stored as a Docker image label (`org.egg.build-hash`).

key_components.name: compute_build_hash()
key_components.description: Computes SHA256 of all build-affecting files including Dockerfile, entrypoint.py, docker-setup.py, pyproject.toml, and all runtime directories. Includes UID/GID. Does NOT currently include any config files or repo-specific files.

key_components.name: create_dockerfile()
key_components.description: Stages build context into ~/.cache/egg/. Copies sandbox files (docker-setup.py, claude-commands, claude-rules, runtime dirs, entrypoint.py, Dockerfile) and shared/ directory. Does NOT currently copy any repo-specific files.

key_components.name: build_image()
key_components.description: Orchestrates the full build: checks if rebuild needed, calls create_dockerfile(), computes hash, runs docker build with build args (USER_NAME, USER_UID, USER_GID, CLAUDE_CODE_VERSION) and labels.

key_components.name: docker-setup.py
key_components.description: Build-time script that installs core + extra OS packages. Reads repositories.yaml for docker_setup.extra_packages. Runs as root during docker build. Has load_config() and get_extra_packages() functions.

key_components.name: Dockerfile
key_components.description: Ubuntu 22.04 base. Installs dev tools → gh CLI → Python 3.11 → pyyaml → docker-setup.py → Python deps → Claude commands/rules → user creation → Claude Code CLI → runtime COPY → git/gh relocation → entrypoint. The docker-setup.py layer is near the top (line 58-63) for caching stability.

key_components.name: get_extra_packages()
key_components.lines: n/a (function not present — extra_packages only parsed by docker-setup.py)
key_components.description: docker-setup.py independently parses repositories.yaml for docker_setup.extra_packages. repo_config.py does not expose this — the build script loads config directly.

key_components.name: get_local_repos()
key_components.description: Returns list of Path objects from local_repos.paths in repositories.yaml. Used by container setup to mount repos. We need this to locate repo directories from which to copy watch files.

key_components.name: get_repo_setting()
key_components.description: Generic per-repo setting accessor. Looks up repo_settings[repo][setting] with case-insensitive repo matching. Can be used to retrieve build_commands.

approaches.name: Extend docker-setup.py to handle build_commands (Recommended)
approaches.description: Extend the existing docker-setup.py build-time script to also read and execute `build_commands` from all `repo_settings` entries. Watch files are copied into the build context by `create_dockerfile()` from local repo paths. A new Dockerfile layer copies these watch files and runs docker-setup.py with a --build-commands flag (or a separate build-deps phase). The build hash includes watch file contents.

changes.description: Add build_commands example to repo_settings section with watch_files and commands sub-keys
Add get_repo_build_commands(repo) and get_all_build_commands() functions to parse and expose build_commands config

Extend to copy watch files from local repo paths into the build context. For each repo with build_commands, copy watch_files from local_repos.paths into ~/.cache/egg/repo-deps/<repo-name>/. Must resolve repo name to local path.
Extend to hash watch file contents from the build context (the copied repo-deps/ directory). Also hash the build_commands config itself so command changes trigger rebuild.

Add install_build_commands() function that iterates repo_settings, changes to each repo's watch-file directory (as a working dir stand-in), and runs each command. Add get_build_commands() to parse the config.

Add a new layer after the existing docker-setup.py layer that: (1) COPYs the repo-deps/ directory, (2) runs docker-setup.py --build-commands (or a separate script) to execute build commands. This layer must come AFTER Python/Node/Go are installed but BEFORE the frequently-changing COPY . layer.
Document the build_commands feature and its caching behavior

pros: Minimally invasive — extends existing patterns (docker-setup.py already reads config and installs packages)
Docker layer caching works naturally — watch files are COPYd before RUN, so Docker only rebuilds when files change
Single build script handles both OS packages and project dependencies
No new scripts or binaries needed
Build hash system naturally extends to include watch files
cons: docker-setup.py grows in complexity (but still manageable at ~350 lines total)
Watch file resolution requires mapping repo name → local path, which means create_dockerfile() needs to read config

approaches.name: New dedicated build-deps.py script
approaches.description: Create a new sandbox/build-deps.py script specifically for project-level dependency installation. This script would be separate from docker-setup.py (which stays focused on OS packages). The Dockerfile would have a dedicated layer that runs build-deps.py after docker-setup.py.

changes.description: Same as Approach A, plus copy build-deps.py to build context
Same as Approach A, plus include build-deps.py in hash
New script that reads config, iterates repos with build_commands, and executes commands in the watch-file directories
Add COPY + RUN layer for build-deps.py

pros: Clean separation of concerns — OS packages vs project dependencies
cons: Adds a new file to maintain
Duplicates config loading logic from docker-setup.py
Slightly more Dockerfile complexity (another COPY + RUN layer)

approaches.name: Dynamic Dockerfile generation with per-repo COPY+RUN layers
approaches.description: Instead of a static Dockerfile, dynamically generate Dockerfile content in create_dockerfile() that includes per-repo COPY and RUN instructions. Each repo's watch files would get their own COPY layer, and each repo's commands would get their own RUN layer. This maximizes cache granularity — changing repo A's lockfile only rebuilds repo A's deps.

changes.description: Major rework: instead of copying a static Dockerfile, generate Dockerfile content dynamically. Read config, for each repo with build_commands, emit COPY + RUN lines.
Convert to a template or generate entirely in Python

pros: Changing one repo's deps doesn't rebuild another's
cons: Significantly more complex — Dockerfile becomes dynamically generated
Harder to debug (generated Dockerfiles are opaque)
Breaks the current pattern of static Dockerfile copied to build context
Over-engineering for the typical 1-3 repos case

recommendation_justification: Approach A extends existing patterns with minimal complexity. The docker-setup.py script already reads repositories.yaml and installs packages — adding build_commands handling is a natural extension. Docker layer caching still works well because all watch files are COPYd in a single layer before the RUN. For the typical 1-3 repos case, the cache invalidation difference vs. per-repo layers (Approach C) is negligible, and the simplicity advantage is significant. Approach B is reasonable but creates unnecessary separation for what is conceptually the same operation (installing things at build time).

tasks.title: Add build_commands to config schema and parser
tasks.description: Add build_commands (with watch_files and commands sub-keys) to repo_settings in repositories.yaml.example. Add get_repo_build_commands(repo) and get_all_build_commands() to config/repo_config.py. Include validation (watch_files must be a list of strings, commands must be a list of strings).

tasks.title: Copy watch files into build context
tasks.description: Extend create_dockerfile() to: (1) read build_commands config for all repos, (2) resolve each repo name to a local path via local_repos.paths (matching by repo name == directory name), (3) copy each repo's watch_files from the local path into ~/.cache/egg/repo-deps/<repo-name>/. Handle missing watch files gracefully (warn but don't fail). The repo-deps/ directory in the build context will be the working directory during build commands.
tasks.design_notes: Mapping repo name (e.g., 'your-org/web-app') to a local path requires scanning local_repos.paths for a directory whose name matches the repo part after '/'. If a repo is in repo_settings but not in local_repos.paths, skip it with a warning (it won't have watch files to copy).

tasks.title: Extend build hash to include watch files and build_commands config
tasks.description: Extend compute_build_hash() to: (1) hash the contents of all watch files copied to the build context (repo-deps/ directory), (2) hash the build_commands configuration itself (serialized as JSON). This ensures that changes to either the watch files or the commands trigger a rebuild.

tasks.title: Extend docker-setup.py to execute build_commands
tasks.description: Add install_build_commands() function to docker-setup.py. It should: (1) read build_commands from all repo_settings entries, (2) for each repo with build_commands, cd to /tmp/repo-deps/<repo-name>/ (where watch files were copied), (3) execute each command sequentially via subprocess, (4) handle failures gracefully (log and continue or fail depending on a strict flag). Also add get_build_commands() to parse the config. The main() function should call install_build_commands() after install_extra_packages().
tasks.design_notes: Commands run as root during build. The working directory is the watch-file directory, which has the dependency files (package-lock.json, requirements.txt, etc.) but NOT the full repo source. Commands like 'npm ci' or 'pip install -r requirements.txt' work fine with just these files. Commands like 'make deps' that need a Makefile would need that file listed in watch_files. Installed packages go to system paths (/usr/lib, /usr/local/lib, node_modules may need special handling — see design decisions).

tasks.title: Add Dockerfile layer for repo dependency installation
tasks.description: Add a new layer to the Dockerfile that: (1) COPYs repo-deps/ directory into /tmp/repo-deps/ (before the RUN command, enabling Docker layer caching on watch file contents), (2) runs docker-setup.py with a --build-commands flag (or unconditionally — it can detect if there are build_commands to run). This layer should be placed after Python/Node/Go toolchains are installed (after the existing docker-setup.py layer and Python deps layers) but before the frequently-changing COPY . layer.
tasks.design_notes: The repo-deps/ COPY must come before the RUN so Docker can cache on file content changes. If no repos have build_commands, the directory will be empty and the layer will be a no-op (fast). The existing docker-setup.py execution (line 58-63) installs OS packages. The new layer runs dependency commands after toolchains are available.

tasks.title: Add tests for new functionality
tasks.description: Add tests for: (1) get_repo_build_commands() and get_all_build_commands() in config, (2) watch file copying logic in create_dockerfile(), (3) build hash changes when watch files or build_commands change, (4) docker-setup.py get_build_commands() and install_build_commands() (mocked subprocess). Follow existing test patterns in tests/sandbox/test_docker.py and tests/sandbox/test_docker_setup.py.

tasks.title: Update documentation
tasks.description: Update sandbox/README.md with build_commands documentation. Update config/repositories.yaml.example with comprehensive examples. Add inline comments to the Dockerfile explaining the new layer.

design_decisions.question: How to map repo names to local paths for watch file copying
design_decisions.decision: Match the repo name (part after '/') against local_repos.paths directory names. For 'your-org/web-app', look for a directory named 'web-app' in local_repos.paths. If multiple matches exist, use the first. If no match, skip with a warning.
design_decisions.rationale: This is the simplest approach that works for the common case. The local_repos.paths list already contains the local paths to repos. Directory names conventionally match the repo name. Edge cases (same repo name in different orgs) are rare and can be handled later if needed.
alternatives_considered: Add an explicit local_path to repo_settings — more explicit but adds config burden
Use git remote to match — requires git access during build which isn't available

design_decisions.question: Where do dependency artifacts go (node_modules, venv, etc.)
design_decisions.decision: Dependencies install to system-global paths during build. npm ci installs to /tmp/repo-deps/<repo>/node_modules (then the actual node_modules is populated at runtime when the repo is mounted). pip install goes to system site-packages. The build is about pre-populating caches and system packages, not about creating working directories.
design_decisions.rationale: The repos are mounted at runtime, not during build. Build commands that produce directory-local artifacts (like node_modules in the repo directory) won't persist because the build directory is /tmp/repo-deps/. For pip, this works naturally (packages go to system site-packages). For npm, users should use --global or the npm cache will be warm so runtime install is fast. For Python venvs, pip install to system packages is the intended use.
design_decisions.note: This is a key UX consideration: users need to understand that build_commands operate in a directory with ONLY the watch files, not the full repo. Commands should install to system paths. Document this clearly.

design_decisions.question: Should build_commands failure be fatal?
design_decisions.decision: Default to non-fatal (warn and continue), matching the existing extra_packages behavior (check=False on line 152 of docker-setup.py). Log the failure clearly but don't abort the entire build.
design_decisions.rationale: Build failures for one repo shouldn't prevent the container from starting. The user will see the warning in build output and can fix their commands. This matches the existing extra_packages behavior.

design_decisions.question: Where to place the new Dockerfile layer
design_decisions.decision: Place after the Python dependencies layer (after line 104) and before the Claude commands COPY (line 111). This ensures Python, Node (if installed via extra_packages), and other toolchains are available when build commands run.
design_decisions.rationale: Build commands like 'pip install -r requirements.txt' need Python available. Commands like 'npm ci' need Node available (installed via extra_packages). Placing the layer after all toolchain installations but before the frequently-changing layers maximizes caching benefit.

design_decisions.question: How to pass config to docker-setup.py for the build_commands phase
design_decisions.decision: docker-setup.py already loads config via load_config(). For build_commands, it reads from the same config. The repo-deps/ directory is at a known path (/tmp/repo-deps/) inside the container during build. No additional config mechanism needed.
design_decisions.rationale: Reuses the existing config loading pattern. The config file is already accessible during build (repositories.yaml is in the host's ~/.config/egg/ and can be mounted or copied to build context if needed).
design_decisions.note: Important consideration: during docker build, repositories.yaml may not be at the standard path. Currently docker-setup.py tries multiple paths including ~/repos/egg/config/repositories.yaml. We may need to COPY the config into the build context (create_dockerfile would handle this) or pass build_commands as a build arg.

design_decisions.question: How to pass build_commands configuration into the Docker build
design_decisions.decision: Write a build-commands.json manifest to the build context (alongside Dockerfile) that contains all repos' build_commands. docker-setup.py reads this file instead of parsing repositories.yaml for build commands. create_dockerfile() generates this manifest.
design_decisions.rationale: repositories.yaml may not be available during docker build (it's a host-side config file). Rather than COPYing the entire config (which contains tokens and sensitive info), we generate a minimal manifest with only the build-relevant data. This also decouples the build script from the full config schema. The manifest approach is already used for other build-time data passing.

risks_and_mitigations.risk: Build commands may fail in the watch-file-only directory
risks_and_mitigations.mitigation: Document clearly that the working directory contains only watch_files, not the full repo. Provide examples showing which commands work (pip install -r, npm ci) vs which don't (make with source deps). Consider adding a note about 'npm ci --ignore-scripts' for Node projects that have post-install scripts requiring source.

risks_and_mitigations.risk: Stale watch files if user forgets to rebuild after changing deps
risks_and_mitigations.mitigation: The build hash system handles this automatically — compute_build_hash() will include watch file contents, so running egg will detect changes and trigger a rebuild.

risks_and_mitigations.risk: Config not available during Docker build
risks_and_mitigations.mitigation: Use the build-commands.json manifest approach (DD-6). create_dockerfile() generates the manifest from host-side config. The manifest is COPY'd into the build context. docker-setup.py reads the manifest, not the raw config.

risks_and_mitigations.risk: Node.js/Go/other runtimes may not be installed when build_commands run
risks_and_mitigations.mitigation: Document that runtimes must be installed first (via docker_setup.extra_packages or the Dockerfile base layers). The Dockerfile layer order ensures Python is always available. For Node, users need to add nodejs to extra_packages.apt. Consider adding a validation warning at build time if a build command uses a tool that isn't in the image.

risks_and_mitigations.risk: Security — arbitrary command execution during build
risks_and_mitigations.mitigation: Commands come from the user's own repositories.yaml, which is a trusted configuration file. This is no different from the existing extra_packages feature which runs apt install with user-specified packages. The build runs in Docker with no access to host secrets beyond the config file.

open_questions.question: Should npm dependencies be installed globally or should we use a persistent npm cache?
open_questions.context: npm ci installs to ./node_modules relative to the working directory. During build, the working directory is /tmp/repo-deps/<repo>/ which has package.json and package-lock.json. The resulting node_modules won't be in the right place at runtime when the actual repo is mounted. Options: (a) install to a global npm prefix, (b) warm the npm cache so runtime 'npm ci' is fast, (c) install to a well-known path and symlink at container startup.
open_questions.recommendation: Option (b) — warm the npm cache. Run 'npm ci' during build (even though node_modules goes to /tmp/repo-deps/), which populates the npm cache. Then at runtime, 'npm ci' reads from cache and is near-instant. This is the most robust approach.

open_questions.question: Should we support a 'run_as' option for build commands (root vs user)?
open_questions.context: docker-setup.py runs as root. Some package managers (npm) prefer non-root execution. pip works fine as root. Go modules work as either.
open_questions.recommendation: Start with root-only (matching existing pattern). Add run_as support later if users request it. Root is simpler and works for all common cases.
